newsitem.title: UK: Major seeks to pick up pieces after bad 1997 start.
newsitem.headline: Major seeks to pick up pieces after bad 1997 start.

text.p: After suffering an embarrassing start to 1997, Prime Minister John Major will on Tuesday make a new effort to kick into life his campaign to stay in power in Britain's upcoming general election.

He will hold the first of a series of news conferences (eds; starts 1130 GMT) ahead of the formal election campaign in what aides say is a conscious imitation of the strategy of U.S. President Bill Clinton, who was re-elected in November.
Unlike Clinton, Major's party is some 20 points behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls with less than five months to go before the voters make their choice.
Major has been embarrassed in the first week of the new year over two members of parliament of his Conservative Party.

While he is promoting the Conservatives as the party of the family and family values, Jerry Hayes was forced to deny a report in a newspaper that he had had a 16-month affair with a teenage male parliamentary researcher.

The another Conservative legislator, Hugh Dykes, volunteered to join in policy talks being held by the two main opposition parties the day after Major had denounced the same talks as "profoundly dangerous".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats are discussing the possibility of sweeping changes to Britain's constitution, including instituting a bill of rights, having parliaments for Scotland and Wales and perhaps even adopting a voting system of proportional representation.
Dykes insisted his move was not a prelude to leaving the Conservatives and joining one of the other parties, as three of his former colleagues have done over the past two years.
"I am a member of the Tory (Conservative) tribe. I know all the war dances and I use the Tory greasepaint," he said.
But his decision blunted Conservative efforts to suggest that such constitutional changes would destabilise Britain.
"John Major looks even more isolated than ever in his lonely opposition to taking Britain's constitution out of the 19th century," Labour deputy leader John Prescott said.

The Hayes affair follows a series of sexual and financial scandals involving Conservative MPs since the last general election in 1992 which have combined with squabbling over policy to enfeeble the party which has ruled Britain since 1979.

Public relations impresario Max Clifford, who helped the former parliamentary researcher Paul Stone to publicise his allegations against Hayes, said he planned further damaging revelations in the weeks ahead.

Clifford, who has a severely disabled daughter suffering from rheumatoid arthritis, said he was conducting a "personal vendetta" against the Conservatives in a protest against the way they had managed the National Health Service.
Major believes his outgoing meet-the-people style of campaigning helped his party to a narrow surprise victory in 1992 and hopes he can pull it off again.

Aides said that at Tuesday's news conference he planned to attack Labour leader Tony Blair for failing to spell out his policies in detail and to trumpet the health of the British economy, which has been growing rapidly for two years.
